title: The Tomato Test
author: Dr. Chris Hobbs
summary: Chris Hobbs uses the saying that knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit while wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad to ask how Christian schools should respond to new technology, especially artificial intelligence. He reads Job 28 as a lens, noting that people could overturn mountains with mining technology yet still could not find wisdom, and he distinguishes Aristotle's sophia, what is true, from phronesis, what is best to do. Schools, he says, sit at the centre of every societal shift, and Christian schools carry an extra responsibility to model wisdom. He offers five marks of a wise institution: pause before you plunge, put formation first, honor the work by letting technology lift drudgery but never remove demand, own your thinking because whatever is offloaded atrophies, and discern features from bugs. The closing call is for educators to apply wisdom to innovation rather than shun it.
points: The tomato test frames the school's task as teaching students when not to use a capable tool, not just how to use it.
Hobbs separates dominion, drudgery and demand in work, so technology may lighten drudgery but should not remove the effort where growth happens.
Because offloaded thinking atrophies, he recommends sharpening question-asking rather than settling for readily available answers.
Formation comes first, since everything a school engages with does something to its students and early impressions last longest.
The bugs and features example, that bigger homes pulled families apart, warns that efficiency can remove what forms us.
quotes: Aristotle divided knowing into two kinds. Sophia concerns what is true. Phronesis asks a different question: what is the best thing to do here?
Knowledge is knowing a tomato is a fruit. Wisdom is knowing not to put it in a fruit salad.
Then he flips the script. For all that their technology allowed them to discover, they still could not find wisdom.
A wise school never loses sight of a priority higher than the mere accumulation of information or students’ achievement.
We should never use technology to remove demand, because demand is where dominion is produced.
One of the great hazards of the coming age of artificial intelligence is simple: whatever we offload will atrophy.
In trying to eliminate a bug, we eliminated the very feature that nurtured close families: proximity.
